description: Master modern C++ features such as RAII, templates, and concurrency patterns that power high-performance systems.

days.title: Day 25 – C++ List (Doubly Linked List)
days.definition: List is a sequence container that allows fast insertion/deletion anywhere, implemented as doubly linked list.
days.explanation: List is like a chain where each link knows its neighbors. Easy to add/remove links anywhere.
days.real_world_example: Used in music playlists, browser history, undo/redo operations.
interactive_tasks: Create list of integers
Add/remove from both ends

quiz.question: Can list access elements by index?
quiz.reasoning: List doesn't support random access by index.

quiz.question: Where can you add elements in list?
quiz.reasoning: List supports insertion anywhere.

quiz.question: How is list implemented?
quiz.reasoning: List uses doubly linked nodes.

days.title: Day 26 – C++ Stack (LIFO)
days.definition: Stack is a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) container where elements are added/removed only from top.
days.explanation: Stack is like a pile of plates - you add/remove from top only. Last plate added is first removed.
days.real_world_example: Used in function calls, undo operations, expression evaluation, browser back button.
interactive_tasks: Create stack of integers
Implement simple undo system

quiz.question: What does LIFO mean?
quiz.reasoning: LIFO = Last element added is first removed.

quiz.question: Where are elements added in stack?
quiz.reasoning: Stack only allows top operations.

quiz.question: Which function removes top element?
quiz.reasoning: pop() removes top element.

days.title: Day 27 – C++ Map (Key-Value Pairs)
days.definition: Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys, providing fast lookup by key.
days.explanation: Map is like a dictionary - look up word (key) to find meaning (value). Each word appears once.
days.real_world_example: Used in phone books (name→number), dictionaries (word→meaning), configurations (setting→value).
interactive_tasks: Create map for student grades
Make phone directory

quiz.question: What does map store?
quiz.reasoning: Map stores pairs of keys and values.

quiz.question: Are map keys unique?
quiz.reasoning: Each key must be unique in map.

quiz.question: How to access map value?
quiz.reasoning: Values are accessed by their keys.

days.title: Day 28 – C++ STL Algorithms
days.definition: STL Algorithms are pre-built functions in the <algorithm> library that perform common operations like sorting, searching, and manipulating data structures using iterators.
days.explanation: STL Algorithms are like power tools for programmers. Instead of writing repetitive loops for sorting or searching, you use these ready-made, optimized functions. They work with any data structure that supports iterators (like vectors, lists, arrays). Think of them as a toolbox: sort() is your hammer, find() is your screwdriver, and transform() is your power drill. They make your code shorter, faster, and less error-prone.
days.real_world_example: STL Algorithms are used everywhere: Sorting products by price on e-commerce sites, searching for users in databases, filtering spam emails, ranking search results, processing sensor data in IoT devices, and analyzing financial data. When you sort contacts in your phone, when you search for a file on your computer, when a website filters products - all these use algorithms similar to STL algorithms.
interactive_tasks: Create a vector of 10 random numbers and sort them in descending order
Find all prime numbers in a vector using find_if algorithm
Use transform to convert a vector of Celsius temperatures to Fahrenheit

quiz.question: Which header file is needed for STL algorithms?
quiz.reasoning: The <algorithm> header contains most STL algorithm functions.

quiz.question: What does sort() function do by default?
quiz.reasoning: sort() uses the < operator by default, which results in ascending order.

quiz.question: Which algorithm finds a specific value in a container?
quiz.reasoning: find() searches for a specific value and returns an iterator to it.

quiz.question: What is required before using binary_search()?
quiz.reasoning: binary_search() works only on sorted ranges.

quiz.question: Which algorithm adds all elements of a container?
quiz.reasoning: accumulate() computes the sum (or other operation) of all elements.

quiz.question: What does transform() algorithm do?
quiz.reasoning: transform() applies a given function to each element and stores results.

quiz.question: Which function finds the smallest element?
quiz.reasoning: min_element() returns iterator to the smallest element.

days.title: Day 29 – C++ STL (Standard Template Library)
days.definition: STL provides ready-to-use data structures and algorithms for efficient programming.
days.explanation: STL is like a toolbox with containers (boxes for data) and tools (algorithms) to work with them.
days.real_world_example: Used in games for enemy lists, in websites for user data, in apps for storing information.
interactive_tasks: Create vector of strings
Use sort on custom data

quiz.question: What does STL stand for?
quiz.reasoning: STL = Standard Template Library.

quiz.question: Which is NOT STL container?
quiz.reasoning: printf is C function, not STL container.

quiz.question: What does vector provide?
quiz.reasoning: Vector is resizable array.

days.title: Day 30 – C++ Namespaces
days.definition: Namespaces are containers that group related code elements together under a unique name to prevent naming conflicts and organize code logically.
days.explanation: Namespaces are like family surnames in a large city. Imagine two people named 'Ali' - one might be 'Ali Khan' and another 'Ali Ahmed'. The surnames (namespaces) help distinguish between them. Similarly, in programming, namespaces prevent conflicts when different libraries or code sections use the same identifier names. They're like virtual folders that keep your code organized and avoid collisions.
days.real_world_example: Namespaces are used extensively in real projects: The C++ Standard Library uses 'std' namespace, game engines use namespaces like 'Physics', 'Graphics', 'Audio', large applications use 'CompanyName::ModuleName::SubModule' structure, and third-party libraries use their own namespaces to avoid conflicts. When you write 'std::cout' or 'sf::RenderWindow' (SFML library), you're using namespaces.
interactive_tasks: Create a 'Geometry' namespace with classes for Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle
Create two namespaces 'English' and 'Spanish' with greeting functions
Create nested namespaces for a school management system

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of namespaces?
quiz.reasoning: Namespaces prevent different code sections from having naming collisions.

quiz.question: Which operator is used to access namespace members?
quiz.reasoning: The scope resolution operator (::) accesses namespace elements.

quiz.question: What does 'using namespace std;' do?
options: Imports all std functions without std:: prefix
quiz.answer: Imports all std functions without std:: prefix
quiz.reasoning: It brings all std namespace members into current scope.

quiz.question: When should you avoid 'using namespace std;'?
quiz.reasoning: It can cause name conflicts in these situations.

quiz.question: What is an anonymous namespace?
quiz.reasoning: Anonymous namespace has no name and is file-specific.

quiz.question: How to create a namespace alias?
quiz.reasoning: This syntax creates a shorter name for a namespace.

quiz.question: What is the benefit of nested namespaces?
quiz.reasoning: They create logical hierarchies for complex projects.

days.title: Day 31 – C++ Keywords Complete Guide
days.definition: Keywords are reserved words in C++ that have special meaning to the compiler and cannot be used as identifiers (variable names, function names, etc.).
days.explanation: Keywords are like the grammar rules of C++ language. Just as you can't use punctuation marks as words in English, you can't use keywords as variable names in C++. They are the building blocks that tell the compiler what you want to do: create loops (for, while), make decisions (if, else), define data types (int, double), control access (public, private), and much more. Understanding keywords is essential for writing correct C++ code.
days.real_world_example: Keywords are used in every C++ program: When you create a variable (int, double), control program flow (if, for), define classes (class, public, private), handle errors (try, catch), manage memory (new, delete), or create templates (template). In game development, 'virtual' enables polymorphism for game objects. In system programming, 'volatile' is used for hardware registers. In large projects, 'namespace' organizes code.
interactive_tasks: Create a program using at least 15 different C++ keywords
Write a class demonstrating public, private, and protected access
Create a template function that works with multiple data types

quiz.question: Which keyword cannot be used as a variable name?
quiz.reasoning: All keywords are reserved and cannot be used as identifiers.

quiz.question: What does the 'virtual' keyword do?
quiz.reasoning: virtual allows function overriding in derived classes.

quiz.question: Which keyword is used for dynamic memory allocation?
quiz.reasoning: new allocates memory dynamically in C++.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of 'const' keyword?
quiz.reasoning: const can make variables unchangeable or indicate const member functions.

quiz.question: Which keyword is an alternative to '&&'?
quiz.reasoning: and is an alternative token for && operator.

quiz.question: What does 'typedef' do?
quiz.reasoning: typedef creates an alias for an existing type.

quiz.question: Which keyword is used in exception handling?
quiz.reasoning: try is used to enclose code that might throw exceptions.

days.title: Day 32 – Resource Management, RAII & Move Semantics
days.definition: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) ties resource lifetime to object lifetime, while move semantics allow efficient transfers without deep copies.

explanation.main: Every resource should be owned by a smart RAII wrapper. Move semantics keep operations efficient by stealing rather than copying ownership.
key_points: Prefer std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr over raw pointers
Implement copy/move constructors alongside assignment operators
Use std::move when transfer of ownership is intended
std::lock_guard and std::scoped_lock automatically unlock mutexes

days.real_world_example: Game engines and graphics libraries use RAII wrappers for textures, shaders, and GPU buffers to avoid leaks under exceptions.
interactive_tasks: Wrap a legacy C API in a class that uses RAII to manage handles
Implement copy, move constructors, and assignment for a Matrix struct
Convert a codebase that uses raw new/delete into smart pointers

quiz.question: What does RAII guarantee?
options: Resources are freed when scope exits
Objects never go out of scope
Memory is only allocated, never freed
quiz.answer: Resources are freed when scope exits
quiz.reasoning: RAII ties acquisition/destruction to constructors/destructors.

quiz.question: What does std::move do?
quiz.reasoning: std::move produces an rvalue reference, enabling move constructors.

quiz.question: Which guard helps with automatic mutex unlocking?
quiz.reasoning: lock_guard releases the mutex when it goes out of scope.

learning_objectives: Identify when to default/delete copy/move constructors
Use smart pointers to avoid manual delete
Ensure mutexes unlock even during exceptions
tips: Favor RAII wrappers over manual cleanup
Use std::move only when you know ownership is transferred

days.title: Day 33 – Templates, Concepts & Compile-Time Introspection
days.definition: Advanced templates unlock generic algorithms that work across types, with Concepts and constexpr enabling compile-time guarantees.

explanation.main: Combine templates with Concepts to express requirements, and use constexpr to compute invariants during compilation.
key_points: Write Concepts that document template expectations
Use constexpr functions for compile-time evaluation
Leverage std::type_traits and SFINAE for conditional logic
Template specialization customizes behavior per type

days.real_world_example: Template-based logging systems choose formatters via Concepts, ensuring only types supporting streaming can be logged.
interactive_tasks: Define a Concept for container-like types and constrain a template function
Implement constexpr factorial and verify at compile time
Use type_traits to detect if a type has a .size() method

quiz.question: What is a C++ Concept?
quiz.reasoning: Concepts describe the requirements a type must satisfy for a template.

quiz.question: What does constexpr do?
quiz.reasoning: constexpr guarantees a function can run at compile time when given constant arguments.

quiz.question: Which trait helps detect if a type is integral?
quiz.reasoning: std::is_integral is a type trait checking for integral types.

learning_objectives: Write Concepts to document template requirements
Use constexpr to precompute expensive results
Apply type traits for conditional compilation

sections.heading: Template Strategies
content: Use Concepts over tag dispatch when possible
Keep templates readable by splitting logic into helper functions
Prefer constexpr if you need branching during compilation

tips: Comment the intent of template constraints for other developers
Use static_assert to provide helpful compile-time messages

days.title: Day 34 – Concurrency, Coroutines & Patterns
days.definition: Modern concurrency combines threads, futures, and coroutines to build responsive systems without data races.

explanation.main: Use structured concurrency, prefer task-based APIs, and let coroutines describe asynchronous flows naturally.
key_points: std::async and std::future for lightweight tasks
Thread pools keep CPU utilization predictable

days.real_world_example: Web servers use futures and coroutines to handle thousands of requests concurrently while keeping each handler readable.
interactive_tasks: Combine std::async tasks with std::future::wait_for timeout handling
Protect shared data with scoped_lock inside a producer/consumer queue
Sketch a coroutine-based pipeline that loads, processes, and stores data

quiz.question: What ensures multiple mutexes unlock safely?
quiz.reasoning: scoped_lock can lock multiple mutexes without deadlock.

quiz.question: What does std::async return?
quiz.reasoning: std::async returns a future that represents the asynchronous result.

quiz.question: Which keyword is used in coroutines to suspend execution?
quiz.reasoning: co_await pauses a coroutine until the awaited operation completes.

learning_objectives: Structure code around tasks instead of raw threads
Avoid data races using scoped locks
Understand coroutine syntax and when to use it

sections.heading: Concurrency Workflow
content: Launch tasks with std::async or a thread pool
Use scoped_lock when multiple mutexes are involved

tips: Keep async tasks short to reduce scheduling overhead
Use co_await only when you have an asynchronous producer/consumer pipeline
